prior_locality_review.evidence: The church symbol lies south of a small coastal brook and north of Rory Chisholm's Brook. The two brooks, coastline and southern inlet constrain the district. The parish's own history provides a candidate institutional identity, St. Andrew's. Restored Highway 19 follows the same broad north-south corridor beside the church search area. Janette MacDonald's 1968 St. Francis Xavier history explicitly places the present stone church where its predecessor stood, supporting reuse of the church site. Local review on September 6 corrects the church to the east side of Highway 19. OpenStreetMap node 1325630467 identifies St. Andrew’s Catholic Parish Church there and supplies the corrected preview point.
prior_locality_review.contradictions: The frozen source-symbol transform placed the church west of Highway 19; that point is rejected for the church preview. The modern church reference is approximately 169 ground metres north-northeast of that prediction and east of the highway. Source pixels and the sheet transform remain unchanged. This locally reviewed placement does not establish the exact historical footprint. Accounts disagree on completion of the wooden predecessor: MacDonald gives 1879; the Participaper gives 1860.
prior_locality_review.next: Compare a pre-1919 photograph or church plan with the present building to resolve the footprint; investigate the conflicting wooden-church completion dates.

external_sources.finding: Two wooden churches preceded the present sandstone church; page does not establish continuity of footprint.

external_sources.source_role: 1968 local history by Janette MacDonald, submitted to St. Francis Xavier University; digitized excerpt preserved by Library and Archives Canada
external_sources.finding: Explicitly places the stone church where its predecessor stood. Records the 1919 lightning fire, cornerstone on Dominion Day 1924, and consecration in August 1927. Supports site continuity, not identical foundations.

external_sources.finding: Reports Father Ronald McDonald building a Gothic church at Judique with hand-cut native stone and a planned copper roof. Confirms construction context, not the predecessor footprint.

Places the replacement wooden church farther from the shore, with a new graveyard, and gives completion in 1860; this conflicts with MacDonald's 1879 date. Reports the 1919 fire and 1924-1927 stone replacement.
